en: Saṃyutta Nikāya 33.1 (SN 33.1, PTS SN iii 257) 1. Vacchagottavagga Rūpa-aññāṇa-sutta (The Discourse on Ignorance of Form) At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, when there is ignorance regarding form, and there is no knowledge of its origin, its cessation, and the way leading to its cessation, one does not know form as it really is; one does not know the arising and passing away of form as it really is; one does not know the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to form as it really is. “When there is ignorance regarding feeling… perception… volitional formations… consciousness, and there is no knowledge of its origin, its cessation, and the way leading to its cessation, one does not know consciousness as it really is; one does not know the arising and passing away of consciousness as it really is; one does not know the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to consciousness as it really is. “Bhikkhus, when there is ignorance regarding form, and there is no knowledge of its origin, its cessation, and the way leading to its cessation, one is not freed from birth, aging, and death; one is not freed from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; one is not freed from suffering, I say. “When there is ignorance regarding feeling… perception… volitional formations… consciousness, and there is no knowledge of its origin, its cessation, and the way leading to its cessation, one is not freed from birth, aging, and death; one is not freed from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; one is not freed from suffering, I say.”
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then the wanderer Vacchagotta approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the wanderer Vacchagotta said this to the Blessed One:
“Master Gotama, what is the cause, what is the reason, for the arising of these various speculative views in the world:
that the world is eternal, or that the world is not eternal; that the world is finite, or that the world is infinite;
that the soul and the body are the same, or that the soul and the body are different; or that a Tathāgata exists after death?”

“Or: ‘The Tathāgata exists after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’?

“Vaccha, it is because of ignorance regarding form, ignorance regarding the arising of form, ignorance regarding the cessation of form, and ignorance regarding the practice leading to the cessation of form.”
Thus these various kinds of speculative views arise in the world:
"The world is eternal," or ...
[as before] ... "A Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death."
“This, Vaccha, is the cause, this is the condition, for these various speculative views that arise in the world:
‘The world is eternal’ or ‘the world is not eternal’ …pe… or ‘a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.’”
First.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 33.2 (SN 33.2, PTS SN iii 258) 1.
Vacchagottavagga (The Chapter on Vacchagotta)
The Discourse on Ignorance Regarding Feeling.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Seated to one side, the wanderer Vacchagotta said this to the Blessed One:
“Master Gotama, what is the cause, what is the reason, for these various speculative views that arise in the world—such as ‘the world is eternal’ or ‘the world is not eternal’ ... pe ...
or ‘a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’?”
“Vaccha, it is through ignorance of feeling, ignorance of the origin of feeling, ignorance of the cessation of feeling,
and ignorance of the practice leading to the cessation of feeling that these various kinds of speculative views arise in the world—
such as ‘the world is eternal’ or ‘the world is not eternal,’ and so forth.”
"Or that 'the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death'.
This, Vaccha, is the cause, this is the condition, for these various speculative views that arise in the world:
"The world is eternal," or "The world is not eternal," and so forth... [as above]... "The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death."
“Or that ‘the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’?
This is the second [discourse]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 33.3 (SN 33.3, PTS SN iii 258).
1. The Chapter on Vacchagotta.
Discourse on the Knowledge of Perception.
Setting at Sāvatthī.
Seated to one side, the wanderer Vacchagotta said this to the Blessed One:
“What, Master Gotama, is the cause, what is the reason, for these various kinds of views that arise in the world—
such as ‘the world is eternal’ or ‘the world is not eternal,’ and so forth?”
“Or that ‘the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’?

“Vaccha, it is because of ignorance regarding perception, ignorance regarding the arising of perception, ignorance regarding the cessation of perception, and ignorance regarding the practice leading to the cessation of perception,
that these various kinds of speculative views arise in the world.”
"Whether the world is eternal, or whether the world is not eternal...
or whether a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.
This, Vaccha, is the cause, this is the condition, for these various kinds of speculative views that arise in the world.
"Or that 'the world is eternal,' or that 'the world is not eternal' ...
or that 'a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.
This is the third [discourse].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 33.4 (SN 33.4, PTS SN iii 259) 1. Vacchagottavagga Saṅkhāraaññāṇasutta (The Discourse on the Lack of Knowledge of Formations) At Sāvatthī. Then the Venerable Vacchagotta approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “Vaccha, when one does not know and does not see things as they really are, one forms a formation; when one knows and sees things as they really are, one does not form a formation. “But, venerable sir, what is it that one does not know and does not see when one forms a formation? “One does not know and does not see, Vaccha, ‘This is suffering’ as it really is; one does not know and does not see ‘This is the origin of suffering’ as it really is; one does not know and does not see ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ as it really is; one does not know and does not see ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’ as it really is. It is when one does not know and does not see these things as they really are that one forms a formation. “But, venerable sir, what is it that one knows and sees when one does not form a formation? “One knows and sees, Vaccha, ‘This is suffering’ as it really is; one knows and sees ‘This is the origin of suffering’ as it really is; one knows and sees ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ as it really is; one knows and sees ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’ as it really is. It is when one knows and sees these things as they really are that one does not form a formation. When this was said, the Venerable Vacchagotta said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir!... From today let the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life. “Vaccha, there are these five aggregates subject to clinging. What five? The aggregate of form subject to clinging, the aggregate of feeling subject to clinging, the aggregate of perception subject to clinging, the aggregate of volitional formations subject to clinging, and the aggregate of consciousness subject to clinging. These are the five aggregates subject to clinging. If, Vaccha, a noble disciple understands as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of these five aggregates subject to clinging, then he is called a noble disciple who is a stream-enterer, no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. When this was said, the Venerable Vacchagotta said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir!... From today let the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life. “Vaccha, there are these six elements. What six? The earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element, the space element, and the consciousness element. These are the six elements. If, Vaccha, a noble disciple understands as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of these six elements, then he is called a noble disciple who is a stream-enterer, no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. When this was said, the Venerable Vacchagotta said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir!... From today let the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life. “Vaccha, there are these six internal and external bases. What six? The eye and forms, the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles, the mind and mental phenomena. These are the six internal and external bases. If, Vaccha, a noble disciple understands as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of these six internal and external bases, then he is called a noble disciple who is a stream-enterer, no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. When this was said, the Venerable Vacchagotta said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir!... From today let the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life. “Vaccha, there are these seven factors of enlightenment. What seven?

The enlightenment factor of mindfulness, the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena, the enlightenment factor of energy, the enlightenment factor of rapture, the enlightenment factor of tranquility, the enlightenment factor of concentration, and the enlightenment factor of equanimity. These are the seven factors of enlightenment. If, Vaccha, a noble disciple understands as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of these seven factors of enlightenment, then he is called a noble disciple who is a stream-enterer, no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. When this was said, the Venerable Vacchagotta said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir!... From today let the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life. “Vaccha, there are these four noble truths. What four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. These are the four noble truths. If, Vaccha, a noble disciple understands as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of these four noble truths, then he is called a noble disciple who is a stream-enterer, no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. When this was said, the Venerable Vacchagotta said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir!... From today let the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life. “Vaccha, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is heading toward Nibbāna with final-knowledge as their destination, the person who is heading toward Nibbāna without final-knowledge as their destination, the person who is heading toward the plane of misery with final-knowledge as their destination, and the person who is heading toward the plane of misery without final-knowledge as their destination. These are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. If, Vaccha, a noble disciple understands as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of these four kinds of persons, then he is called a noble disciple who is a stream-enterer, no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. When this was said, the Venerable Vacchagotta said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir!... From today let the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life. “Vaccha, there are these four nutriments. What four? Physical food as nutriment, gross or subtle; contact as the second nutriment; mental volition as the third nutriment; and consciousness as the fourth nutriment. These are the four nutriments. If, Vaccha, a noble disciple understands as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of these four nutriments, then he is called a noble disciple who is a stream-enterer, no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. When this was said, the Venerable Vacchagotta said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir!... From today let the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life. “Vaccha, there are these four kinds of clinging. What four? Clinging to sensual pleasure, clinging to views, clinging to precepts and observances, and clinging to a doctrine of self. These are the four kinds of clinging. If, Vaccha, a noble disciple understands as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of these four kinds of clinging, then he is called a noble disciple who is a stream-enterer, no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. When this was said, the Venerable Vacchagotta said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir!... From today let the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life. “Vaccha, there are these four kinds of identity view. What four? ‘Material form is my self
At Sāvatthī.
Seated to one side, the wanderer Vacchagotta said this to the Blessed One:
“What, Master Gotama, is the cause, what is the reason, for these various kinds of speculative views that arise in the world?”
“Is the world eternal, or is the world not eternal...
or does the Tathāgata neither exist nor not exist after death?

“Vaccha, it is because of ignorance regarding volitional formations, ignorance regarding the origin of volitional formations, ignorance regarding the cessation of volitional formations, and ignorance regarding the practice leading to the cessation of volitional formations.”
Thus these various kinds of speculative views arise in the world:
"The world is eternal," or "The world is not eternal," and so on,
up to "A Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death."
“This, Vaccha, is the cause, this is the condition, for these various speculative views that arise in the world:
‘The world is eternal’ or ‘the world is not eternal’ …pe… or ‘a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.’”
The Fourth.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 33.5 (SN 33.5, PTS SN iii 259) 1.
Vacchagottavagga (The Chapter on Vacchagotta)
The Discourse on Ignorance Regarding Consciousness.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Seated to one side, the wanderer Vacchagotta said this to the Blessed One:
“Master Gotama, what is the cause, what is the reason, for the arising of these various speculative views in the world—
such as ‘the world is eternal’ or ‘the world is not eternal’ … [and so on] … or ‘a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’?”
“Vaccha, it is through ignorance of consciousness, ignorance of the arising of consciousness, ignorance of the cessation of consciousness,
and ignorance of the way leading to the cessation of consciousness that these various speculative views arise in the world:
‘The world is eternal’ or ‘the world is not eternal’ … [and so on] …”
"Or that 'the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death'?
"Vaccha, this is the cause, this is the reason why these various speculative views arise in the world:
'the world is eternal,' or 'the world is not eternal'... [and so on]..."
“Or that ‘the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’?
This was the fifth.

Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple experiences revulsion toward form, revulsion toward feeling, revulsion toward perception, revulsion toward volitional formations, and revulsion toward consciousness. Experiencing revulsion, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion [his mind] is liberated. When it is liberated there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “Ānanda, if you would abandon desire for whatever is not-self, then by doing so you would abandon desire. By abandoning desire, you would be one who has abandoned desire. By being one who has abandoned desire, you would be one who has abandoned the underlying tendency to lust. By abandoning the underlying tendency to lust, you would be one who has abandoned the underlying tendency to aversion. By abandoning the underlying tendency to aversion, you would be one who has abandoned the underlying tendency to views. By abandoning the underlying tendency to views, you would be one who has abandoned the underlying tendency to doubt. By abandoning the underlying tendency to doubt, you would be one who has abandoned the underlying tendency to conceit. By abandoning the underlying tendency to conceit, you would be one who has abandoned the underlying tendency to desire for existence.

By abandoning the underlying tendency to desire for existence, you would be one who has abandoned the underlying tendency to ignorance. By abandoning the underlying tendency to ignorance, you would be one who has abandoned the underlying tendency to all defilements. When you have abandoned the underlying tendency to all defilements, you would be one who has abandoned birth, aging, and death; one who has abandoned sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; one who has abandoned suffering, I say. “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘When you have abandoned the underlying tendency to all defilements, you would be one who has abandoned birth, aging, and death; one who has abandoned sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; one who has abandoned suffering, I say. Venerable sir, suppose there were a great tree standing possessed of heartwood, and a man would come along bringing a saw. He would cut through the great tree right across at its foot. Having done so, he would split the log lengthwise and hollow it out, making it into a trough. Then, having removed all the inner bark, sapwood, and heartwood, he would carry it off on his head. In the same way, venerable sir, the Blessed One has completely removed the inner bark, sapwood, and heartwood of the great tree of the underlying tendencies. “Ānanda, if you would abandon desire for whatever is not-self, then by doing so you would abandon desire. By abandoning desire, you would be one who has abandoned desire. By being one who has abandoned desire, you would be one who has abandoned the underlying tendency to lust... [as above] ...one who has abandoned suffering, I say. “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘When you have abandoned the underlying tendency to all defilements, you would be one who has abandoned birth, aging, and death; one who has abandoned sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; one who has abandoned suffering, I say. Venerable sir, suppose there were a great tree standing possessed of heartwood, and a man would come along bringing a saw. He would cut through the great tree right across at its foot. Having done so, he would split the log lengthwise and hollow it out, making it into a trough. Then, having removed all the inner bark, sapwood, and heartwood, he would carry it off on his head. In the same way, venerable sir, the Blessed One has completely removed the inner bark, sapwood, and heartwood of the great tree of the underlying tendencies. “Ānanda, if you would abandon desire for whatever is not-self, then by doing so you would abandon desire. By abandoning desire, you would be one who has abandoned desire. By being one who has abandoned desire, you would be one who has abandoned the underlying tendency to lust... [as above] ...one who has abandoned suffering

Saṃyutta Nikāya 33.41–45 (SN 33.41, PTS SN iii 261) 1. Vacchagottavagga The Five Discourses on Non-Regard for Form, etc. (41) Discourse on Non-Regard for Form (42) Discourse on Non-Regard for Feeling (43) Discourse on Non-Regard for Perception (44) Discourse on Non-Regard for Volitional Formations (45) Discourse on Non-Regard for Consciousness At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, form is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self. Thus it should be seen with right wisdom as it really is. “Feeling is impermanent... Perception is impermanent... Volitional formations are impermanent... Consciousness is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self. Thus it should be seen with right wisdom as it really is. “When, bhikkhus, a noble disciple has seen this thus as it really is with right wisdom, he here discards longing for form, discards longing for feeling, discards longing for perception, discards longing for volitional formations, discards longing for consciousness. When he has discarded longing, his mind is inclined toward dispassion; through dispassion it is liberated; when liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. He understands: ‘Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being. [The remaining four discourses repeat the same structure, substituting each of the other aggregates for form.]
At Sāvatthī.
“Vaccha, it is through non-regard for form... [as before] ...it is through non-regard for consciousness, Vaccha...
[as before]. (45)

Saṃyutta Nikāya 33.46–50 (SN 33.46, PTS SN iii 261) 1. Vacchagottavagga The Five Discourses on Non-Regard for Form, etc. (46) Discourse on Non-Regard for Form At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, form is not to be regarded; feeling is not to be regarded; perception is not to be regarded; volitional formations are not to be regarded; consciousness is not to be regarded. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, when one regards form, when one closely examines it, attachment arises; when one does not regard it, when one does not closely examine it, attachment ceases. When one regards feeling… perception… volitional formations… consciousness, when one closely examines it, attachment arises; when one does not regard it, when one does not closely examine it, attachment ceases. Therefore, bhikkhus, form is not to be regarded; feeling is not to be regarded; perception is not to be regarded; volitional formations are not to be regarded; consciousness is not to be regarded. (47) Discourse on Non-Desire for Form At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, form is not to be desired; feeling is not to be desired; perception is not to be desired; volitional formations are not to be desired; consciousness is not to be desired. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, when one desires form, when one longs for it, attachment arises; when one does not desire it, when one does not long for it, attachment ceases. When one desires feeling… perception… volitional formations… consciousness, when one longs for it, attachment arises; when one does not desire it, when one does not long for it, attachment ceases. Therefore, bhikkhus, form is not to be desired; feeling is not to be desired; perception is not to be desired; volitional formations are not to be desired; consciousness is not to be desired. (48) Discourse on Non-Delight in Form At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, form is not to be delighted in; feeling is not to be delighted in; perception is not to be delighted in; volitional formations are not to be delighted in; consciousness is not to be delighted in. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, when one delights in form, when one finds pleasure in it, attachment arises; when one does not delight in it, when one does not find pleasure in it, attachment ceases. When one delights in feeling… perception… volitional formations… consciousness, when one finds pleasure in it, attachment arises; when one does not delight in it, when one does not find pleasure in it, attachment ceases. Therefore, bhikkhus, form is not to be delighted in; feeling is not to be delighted in; perception is not to be delighted in; volitional formations are not to be delighted in; consciousness is not to be delighted in. (49) Discourse on Non-Grasping at Form At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, form is not to be grasped; feeling is not to be grasped; perception is not to be grasped; volitional formations are not to be grasped; consciousness is not to be grasped. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, when one grasps form, when one clings to it, attachment arises; when one does not grasp it, when one does not cling to it, attachment ceases. When one grasps feeling… perception… volitional formations… consciousness, when one clings to it, attachment arises; when one does not grasp it, when one does not cling to it, attachment ceases. Therefore, bhikkhus, form is not to be grasped; feeling is not to be grasped; perception is not to be grasped; volitional formations are not to be grasped; consciousness is not to be grasped. (50) Discourse on Non-Identification with Form At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, form is not to be identified with; feeling is not to be identified with; perception is not to be identified with; volitional formations are not to be identified with; consciousness is not to be identified with. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, when one identifies with form, when one identifies oneself with it, attachment arises; when one does not identify with it, when one does not identify oneself with it, attachment ceases. When one identifies with feeling… perception… volitional formations… consciousness, when one identifies oneself with it, attachment arises; when one does not identify with it, when one does not identify oneself with it, attachment ceases. Therefore, bhikkhus, form is not to be identified with; feeling is not to be identified with; perception is not to be identified with; volitional formations are not to be identified with; consciousness is not to be identified with.”
At Sāvatthī.
“Vaccha, it is through non-regard for form... [as before] ...it is through non-regard for consciousness, Vaccha...
[as before]. (The fiftieth.)

Saṃyutta Nikāya 33.51–54 (SN 33.51, PTS SN iii 261) 1. Vacchagottavagga The Tetrad of Discourses on Not Having Seen Form, etc. (Rūpa-appaccakkhakammādi-suttacatukka) (51) "Bhikkhus, one who has not seen form directly, who has not heard it, who has not sensed it, and who has not cognized it through the mind—such a person does not conceive a conceit regarding form; they do not conceive a conceit regarding feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness. Because they do not conceive a conceit, they do not cling; because they do not cling, they are not fettered. Being unfettered, they have attained final Nibbāna in this very life. This is the escape from form, the escape from feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness. (52) "Bhikkhus, one who has seen form directly, who has heard it, who has sensed it, and who has cognized it through the mind—such a person conceives a conceit regarding form; they conceive a conceit regarding feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness. Because they conceive a conceit, they cling; because they cling, they are fettered. Being fettered, they have not attained final Nibbāna in this very life. This is the bondage to form, the bondage to feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness. (53) "Bhikkhus, one who has not seen form directly, who has not heard it, who has not sensed it, and who has not cognized it through the mind—such a person does not conceive a conceit regarding form; they do not conceive a conceit regarding feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness. Because they do not conceive a conceit, they do not cling; because they do not cling, they are not fettered. Being unfettered, they have attained final Nibbāna in this very life. This is the escape from form, the escape from feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness. (54) "Bhikkhus, one who has seen form directly, who has heard it, who has sensed it, and who has cognized it through the mind—such a person conceives a conceit regarding form; they conceive a conceit regarding feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness. Because they conceive a conceit, they cling; because they cling, they are fettered. Being fettered, they have not attained final Nibbāna in this very life. This is the bondage to form, the bondage to feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness."
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Then the wanderer Vacchagotta approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the wanderer Vacchagotta said this to the Blessed One:
“Master Gotama, what is the cause, what is the reason, for the arising of these various speculative views in the world—
such as ‘the world is eternal’ … [and so on] … or ‘a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’?”

“Vaccha, it is because one has not directly experienced form; one has not directly experienced the arising of form; one has not directly experienced the cessation of form; one has not directly experienced the practice leading to the cessation of form… [as before] … At Sāvatthī.
“Vaccha, it is because one has not directly experienced feeling… [as before] … one has not directly experienced the practice leading to the cessation of feeling… [as before] …”
The setting was at Sāvatthī.

“Vaccha, it is because of not having made perception personally evident that... [as before] ...because of not having made the practice leading to the cessation of perception personally evident that...
The setting was at Sāvatthī.

“Vaccha, it is because of not having direct knowledge regarding volitional formations … [as before] … that one has not directly experienced the practice leading to the cessation of volitional formations … [as before] …” (Fifty-fourth).
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 33.55 (SN 33.55, PTS SN iii 261).
1. The Chapter on Vacchagotta.
Discourse on the Non-Verification of Consciousness.
Setting at Sāvatthī.

“Vaccha, it is because one has not directly experienced consciousness, has not directly experienced the arising of consciousness, has not directly experienced the cessation of consciousness, and has not directly experienced the practice leading to the cessation of consciousness,
that these various kinds of speculative views arise in the world:
‘The world is eternal’ or ‘The world is not eternal’ … [and so on] …”
"Or that 'the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death'—
this, Vaccha, is the cause, this is the condition, for these various speculative views that arise in the world:
that 'the world is eternal,' or 'the world is non-eternal,' or 'the world is finite,' or 'the world is infinite.'"

"Whether it is 'the soul is the same as the body' or 'the soul is one thing and the body another,' or 'a Tathāgata exists after death,' or 'a Tathāgata does not exist after death,' or 'a Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,' or 'a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.'"
Fifty-fifth. The first chapter, the Vacchagotta Chapter.
Its summary verse:
Through lack of knowledge and lack of vision,
through non-realization and non-awakening,
through non-penetration and lack of clear observation.
Non-discrimination is non-apprehension;
non-regard is non-contemplation;
it is the act of non-direct perception.
The Saṃyutta on Vacchagotta is complete.
